etymology: From Old English bringan (to bring, to carry), the agent noun in its plural form; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the account of Jehu's letter to the rulers of Jezreel and Samaria.
biblical_def:
The elders also, and the bringers up of the children, sent to Jehu.

Bringers appears once in the Authorized Version, in the phrase the bringers up of the children, naming those entrusted with the rearing and education of the seventy sons of Ahab left in Samaria after his death. Jehu, moving to exterminate Ahab's house per Elijah's prophecy against it (1Ki 21:21-22), sent a deliberately provoking letter to the rulers, elders, and bringers up of the children, daring them to set the best and meetest of their master's sons on his throne and fight for the house of their lord (2Ki 10:2-3). Terrified by Jehu's reputation and unwilling to stand against him, they instead sent back word we will do all that thou shalt bid us; we will not make any king (2Ki 10:5), and the seventy sons were beheaded the next day at Jehu's command. The bringers up of the children occupied a position of trust and responsibility Scripture takes seriously — men charged with raising the next generation of a royal house — and their answer here is a study in worldly self-preservation rather than covenant loyalty, choosing survival under a new king over any principled stand, whether for good or ill, regarding the household they had been set to raise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BRING UP: to educate, to rear from infancy; the plural agent noun here naming those charged with rearing Ahab's seventy sons in Samaria.
webster_full: BRING UP, v.t. To rear; to educate; to instruct and form the manners of in youth.
BRINGERS, n. plural. Those who bring up or rear; guardians, tutors.

corruption_summary: A reading focused only on Jehu's severity can miss that the bringers up of the children are themselves indicted here for a cowardly self-preservation that abandons the household entrusted to their care rather than standing for anything at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode is sometimes read purely as commentary on Jehu's violence, but the text gives equal weight to the officials' own moral failure: charged with raising the next generation faithfully, they instead hand their charges over the moment loyalty becomes costly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the weight Scripture places on those who raise and teach the young: the office itself is honorable, and its holders are judged by whether they exercise it faithfully when faithfulness is costly, not only when it is easy.

etymology: From Old English brad (broad, wide), the comparative form; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Zophar's speech comparing the unsearchable knowledge of God to the vastness of earth and sea.
biblical_def:
The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.

Broader appears once in the Authorized Version, in Zophar the Naamathite's speech to Job, describing the knowledge of God as a measure exceeding the earth in length and the sea in breadth. Zophar's question just before is direct: canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? (Job 11:7), and his answer, framed in these vast spatial images, is an emphatic no — God's understanding is higher than heaven, deeper than hell, and broader than any measure a man could take with his own instruments. The irony threaded through Job's three friends' speeches is that they speak profound truths about God's incomprehensibility while badly misapplying them to Job's particular suffering, assuming that because God's ways are unsearchable, Job must be hiding some unconfessed sin. The comparison itself, though spoken by a friend whom God later rebukes for not speaking of me the thing that is right (Job 42:7), stands as sound doctrine: no human measuring line, however long, reaches the full extent of God's knowledge and wisdom, a truth the New Testament echoes in Paul's own doxology over the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Rom 11:33).

webster_full: BROAD, adj. Wide; extended from side to side.
BROADER, adj. The comparative degree of broad; wider than another thing compared.

The truth stated is sound doctrine even though Zophar misapplies it to accuse Job wrongly.

corruption_summary: A skeptical reading can use the incomprehensibility of God as grounds to doubt that He can be truly known at all, missing that Scripture pairs His unsearchable vastness with His gracious self-revelation in His Word and in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The vastness Zophar describes, taken alone, can slide into an agnosticism that concludes nothing certain can be known of God; Scripture instead pairs this incomprehensibility with real, sufficient revelation, so that what cannot be exhaustively searched can still be truly and savingly known.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's own, echoing this text: the depth of God's wisdom is unsearchable (Rom 11:33), yet that same God has made Himself known in Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).

etymology: A compound of broken and footed, from Old English brecan and fot; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Levitical law's list of physical defects barring a priest from offering the bread of God.
biblical_def:
Or a man that is brokenfooted, or brokenhanded.

Brokenfooted appears once in the Authorized Version, in Leviticus 21's catalogue of physical blemishes that disqualified a descendant of Aaron from approaching the altar to offer the bread of his God, though he was still permitted to eat of the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy (Lev 21:22). The list is deliberately comprehensive — blind, lame, a flat nose, any thing superfluous, brokenfooted, brokenhanded, crookbackt, a dwarf, a defect in his eye, scurvy, scabbed, or having his stones broken (Lev 21:18-20) — and its purpose is not to shame the men it describes but to guard the holiness of the sanctuary service through a visible, bodily picture of the perfection required to stand before a holy God. The law's provision that such a priest still eats the bread even while barred from offering it is itself a mercy, distinguishing exclusion from the altar's specific function from exclusion from the covenant community and its provision. The whole regulation finds its resolution in Christ, the great High Priest without blemish and without spot (1Pe 1:19, Heb 9:14), whose perfect body fulfilled in reality what these physical requirements could only picture in shadow, and in whom believers, however broken in body, are made a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ (1Pe 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828), a compound of BROKEN and FOOTED: having a fractured or maimed foot; one of the Levitical disqualifications from priestly altar service, though not from eating the priestly bread.
webster_full: BROKEN, adj. Fractured; severed by violence; disabled.
FOOTED, adj. Having feet, here in the compound denoting the state of the foot.

corruption_summary: A reading that takes this law as evidence Scripture despises the physically disabled misses both the law's own mercy, in preserving such a priest's food and place in the covenant, and its typological purpose, pointing to Christ's perfection rather than condemning imperfect men.
corruption_paragraphs: Taken out of its typological context, the law can be read as cruelty toward the disabled; but the text itself provides for the disqualified priest's full provision and covenant standing, distinguishing a specific ceremonial function from any judgment on the man's worth or place among God's people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is typology itself: the physical perfection required of Aaron's priests was never the true point but a shadow of the perfect, unblemished Priest to come, in whom every believer, whatever their bodily condition, is made a priest to offer acceptable spiritual sacrifice (1Pe 2:5).

etymology: A compound of broken and handed, from Old English brecan and hand; appearing once in the Authorized Version, paired with brokenfooted in the Levitical catalogue of priestly disqualifications.
biblical_def:
Or a man that is brokenfooted, or brokenhanded.

Brokenhanded appears once in the Authorized Version, immediately alongside brokenfooted in Leviticus 21's list of physical blemishes barring a son of Aaron from offering the bread of his God at the altar, though not from eating it (Lev 21:22). The pairing of foot and hand in a single verse completes a picture of the whole body's required soundness for altar service — the hand that would lift the offering, the foot that would stand at the altar, both required to be whole for this specific, ceremonial function. As with every item in this list, the disqualification is narrow and specific: it bars the man from one particular office, not from the covenant, not from worship generally, not from God's provision, which remained fully his. The larger pattern in Leviticus is that the sanctuary's furniture, sacrifices, and priests were all held to a standard of physical wholeness that pictured, in shadow, the moral and spiritual perfection no fallen man actually possesses, a perfection Hebrews says the law could never truly give, since the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never... make the comers thereunto perfect (Heb 10:1). Christ's own hands, pierced at Calvary and yet perfectly whole in priestly office, complete what the shadow in Leviticus could only foreshadow.

HANDED, adj. Having hands, here in the compound denoting the state of the hand.

corruption_paragraphs: Applied loosely, the verse risks being used to suggest bodily wholeness measures spiritual standing before God; the text itself resists this by carefully preserving the disqualified priest's food, dignity, and place among the people, restricting the exclusion to the altar function alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the law's own shadow-and-substance structure: physical wholeness in Leviticus pictures moral perfection no man possesses, met only in the perfect priesthood of Christ, whose own pierced hands accomplished what Aaron's whole-handed sons could only foreshadow.

etymology: From Old English byldan (to build), the archaic second-person singular past tense ("thou buildedst"); appearing in the Authorized Version of Moses' warning to Israel before entering the land of promise.
biblical_def:
Great and goodly cities, which thou buildedst not.

Buildedst appears in Deuteronomy, in Moses' address to Israel just before they crossed into the land the LORD had sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — a land of great and goodly cities which thou buildedst not, houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not (Deu 6:10-11). The archaic thou-form is Moses' emphatic, personal address to each Israelite standing on the edge of an inheritance entirely unearned by their own labor — cities they did not build, houses they did not fill, wells they did not dig. The warning that immediately follows names the precise danger of unearned plenty: when thou shalt have eaten and be full; then beware lest thou forget the LORD (Deu 6:11-12). Moses anticipates that prosperity, received as pure gift, is more spiritually dangerous to a covenant people than hardship, because ease tempts the heart to credit itself rather than the Giver. The whole passage stands behind the Shema just given (Deu 6:4-9) as its practical test: love for the LORD with all the heart, soul, and might is proved not in the wilderness where dependence was obvious, but in the goodly cities where forgetting Him becomes easy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), the archaic second-person singular past tense of BUILD: thou didst build; here of the goodly cities Israel would inherit without having labored to build them.
webster_full: BUILD, v.t. To construct; to erect, as an edifice.
BUILDEDST, v. Archaic second-person singular past tense: thou didst build.

corruption_summary: A prosperity-gospel instinct treats unearned blessing as simple proof of favor to be enjoyed without further reflection, exactly inverting Moses' warning that unearned plenty is the specific occasion for forgetting the God who gave it.
corruption_paragraphs: A theology that measures spiritual health by material increase risks repeating precisely the failure Moses warns against here: receiving cities, houses, wells, and vineyards as though self-secured rather than gifted, and forgetting the Giver in the very moment of greatest ease.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Moses' own, immediate and unqualified: the danger is not scarcity but plenty, and the remedy is the Shema just spoken — love for the LORD proved in fullness, not only in want.

etymology: From Old French bois/busche (bush, wood), through Middle English busshi; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the bride's description of her beloved in the Song of Solomon.
biblical_def:
His head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven.

Bushy appears once in the Authorized Version, in the Song of Solomon, as the Shulamite describes her beloved to the daughters of Jerusalem in a series of vivid, admiring images: his head as fine gold, his locks bushy and black as a raven, his eyes as doves, his cheeks as a bed of spices (Son 5:11-13). The word names hair full, thick, and luxuriant — a mark of youthful vigor and beauty in the ancient Near Eastern imagination, contrasted elsewhere in Scripture with baldness as a picture of diminished strength. The description opens the most extended physical praise of the beloved anywhere in the Song, a poem the Reformed tradition has long read on two levels held together rather than opposed: a genuine, unashamed celebration of marital love and physical beauty within the covenant of marriage, and a typological picture of Christ's beauty and the Church's longing for her Bridegroom. This bushy, raven-black hair belongs to that same register as the rest of the Song's imagery — concrete, sensory, and unembarrassed — a reminder that Scripture nowhere treats physical delight in a spouse as beneath its dignity to describe, provided that delight stays within marriage's proper bounds.

BUSHY, adj. Thick and spreading, as hair or foliage; full, shaggy.

corruption_summary: A prudish reading that treats the Song's physical praise as an embarrassment to be allegorized away entirely misses that Scripture presents marital delight in a spouse's body as itself a good gift, not merely a code for something else.

The text itself gives no such signal; the description is concrete and physical throughout.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Reformed both-and: the Song genuinely celebrates physical, marital love as a good gift from God, while also, without contradiction, foreshadowing Christ's beauty and the Church's longing for Him.

etymology: A compound of by and way, from Old English big/be and weg; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Deborah's song describing the disruption of ordinary travel under Canaanite oppression.
biblical_def:
The highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways.

Byways appears once in the Authorized Version, in the Song of Deborah, describing conditions in Israel before the LORD raised up Deborah as a deliverer: the highways were unoccupied, the ordinary, direct roads abandoned, and travellers walked through byways, the crooked, indirect, hidden paths used to avoid danger. The days of Shamgar and Jael named in the same verse (Jdg 5:6) were days of severe Canaanite oppression under Jabin and his captain Sisera, when Israel's own main roads had become too dangerous for ordinary commerce and travel to continue safely. The byways picture a land under judgment for its idolatry (Jdg 4:1), where basic civic order — safe roads, open travel, ordinary life — had broken down as a direct, visible consequence of covenant unfaithfulness. Deborah's song celebrates precisely the reversal this deliverance brought: by verse 11 the archers are silenced and they that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water rehearse the righteous acts of the LORD, and by implication the highways are free again. The byways stand as one small, concrete detail testifying that when a nation forsakes the LORD, even its roads bear the mark of that forsaking, and when He delivers, even its roads bear the mark of that deliverance.

corruption_summary: A purely political or economic reading of the disrupted roads misses Judges' own diagnosis, which names Israel's idolatry, not merely Canaanite strength, as the root cause of the oppression that made the highways unsafe.
corruption_paragraphs: It is possible to read the byways as evidence only of Canaanite military superiority, a matter of geopolitics rather than covenant. Judges 4:1 names the actual cause first: the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the LORD, and the oppression follows as consequence, not merely circumstance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the book of Judges' own repeating pattern: sin brings oppression, oppression brings crying out, and the LORD in mercy raises up a deliverer, a cycle the byways of Judges 5:6 mark at its lowest point.

etymology: From Old Norse kasta (to throw), the archaic second-person singular past tense ("thou castedst"); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Psalmist's confession of the danger of pride.
biblical_def:
Thou castedst them down into destruction.

Castedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in Psalm 73, Asaph's confession of nearly stumbling over the prosperity of the wicked. Asaph had watched the wicked flourish, proud, violent, and untroubled by the sufferings that afflicted the righteous, until his feet were almost gone, his steps had well nigh slipped (Psa 73:2), envying at the foolish when he saw the prosperity of the wicked (Psa 73:3). The turning point came when he went into the sanctuary of God, and then understood I their end (Psa 73:17) — and the verse containing castedst is precisely that understanding, expressed to God in direct, second-person address: surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. What looked from the outside like stable, enviable prosperity is revealed, from the vantage point of worship and eternity, as a slippery place, a position from which the wicked's own apparent security becomes the very means of their sudden ruin. Asaph's confession moves from near-apostasy through worship to renewed confidence, ending in one of the Psalter's clearest statements of covenant devotion: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee (Psa 73:25).

corruption_paragraphs: A worldly accounting of who is blessed looks only at present ease and concludes the prosperous wicked have the better portion, exactly the envy Asaph confesses nearly overtook him until he saw their end.

etymology: From Old French chalongier (to accuse, to claim), from Latin calumniari; the archaic third-person singular form appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's law of restitution for disputed property.
biblical_def:
Another challengeth to be his, the cause of both parties shall come before the judges.

Challengeth appears once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's law governing disputes over lost or stolen property — ox, ass, sheep, raiment, or any manner of lost thing — when one party claims possession and another challengeth, or lays legal claim, to be his. The law's remedy is deliberately judicial rather than left to private force or accusation: the cause of both parties shall come before the judges, and whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour (Exo 22:9). This is part of a larger body of Mosaic case law, the mishpatim of Exodus 21-23, that translates the moral demands of the Ten Commandments into concrete civil procedure for an actual nation, establishing courts, evidence, and penalties rather than leaving property disputes to whoever could assert a claim most forcefully. The doubled restitution for a false or malicious claim (as for proven theft, Exo 22:4) treats a dishonest legal challenge as itself a form of theft, punishable at the same rate, a safeguard against using the courts themselves as an instrument of injustice against an innocent neighbor. The provision reflects a consistent biblical pattern: God's law does not merely forbid theft in the abstract but builds institutions — judges, evidence, proportionate penalty — that make justice actually operable among sinful people.

corruption_summary: A modern instinct to resolve disputes informally or by whoever asserts a claim most forcefully or loudly misses the law's own insistence that property disputes be settled by established judicial process, with real accountability for a dishonest claim.
corruption_paragraphs: Where disputes are settled by social pressure, reputation, or sheer persistence rather than evidence before an appointed judge, the law's actual safeguard — accountability for a false claim, at real cost to the false claimant — is lost entirely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Exodus's own: God cares about the mechanics of justice, not only its abstract demand, building courts and penalties that make fair resolution actually possible among sinful neighbors.

etymology: From Old French changeable, from changer (to change); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah's catalogue of Jerusalem's luxurious, proud finery.
biblical_def:
The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins.

Changeable appears once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah's long, deliberately exhaustive list of the ornaments and finery the LORD would strip from the daughters of Zion for their haughtiness and pride (Isa 3:16-24) — tinkling ornaments, cauls, round tires, bonnets, and among them the changeable suits of apparel, garments of such variety and abundance that the wearer could change them at will, a mark of conspicuous, ostentatious wealth. Isaiah's charge is not against beauty or fine clothing as such but against the whole posture the list represents: the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go (Isa 3:16), external adornment mirroring internal pride at a moment when the nation stood under coming judgment. The chapter's severe reversal — instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty (Isa 3:24) — strips away every item catalogued in the preceding verses, changeable suits included, as a visible sign that the LORD's judgment reaches what a proud people had most prized. The passage stands as a sober warning that finery worn as a badge of pride, rather than received with gratitude, becomes exactly what judgment is aimed to strip away.

corruption_summary: A reading that treats this passage as blanket condemnation of nice clothing misses that Isaiah's target is explicitly pride and haughtiness, not adornment itself, which Scripture elsewhere commends within proper bounds.
corruption_paragraphs: Applied without its context, the list can be used to condemn any fine possession as inherently sinful; the text itself names the sin precisely as haughtiness and wanton pride (Isa 3:16), not the garments considered apart from the heart that wears them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own diagnosis: it is the proud heart displaying itself through finery that draws judgment, and Proverbs 31's own praise of a virtuous woman's fine clothing (Pro 31:22) shows the issue was never clothing as such.
